name: Lust (luxuria) as capital vice
plainSummary: In this tradition, lust denotes sexual desire disordered by object, circumstance, or intent—treating persons as mere means to appetite.
description: Derived principle: luxuria (lust) is the capital vice of inordinate sexual appetite—desire that ignores temperance, consent, covenant, or the integral good of persons, as classically articulated in Christian sexual ethics.
foundationStrengthRationale: The category is central in traditional manuals of moral theology; modern disputes over consent, marriage, and autonomy make application highly contested.

pros.claim: Highlights objectification and appetite-driven harm that many ethical frameworks also condemn.
pros.evidence: Overlaps with secular concerns about exploitation, coercion, and pornography's incentives.

cons.claim: Traditional definitions often clash with contemporary views on sexual autonomy, LGBTQ dignity, and plural family forms.
cons.evidence: Ongoing moral and legal debates show deep disagreement on what counts as disordered versus healthy desire.
